headline: India's harvest miracle is draining its wells
dek: Norman Borlaug, Mexico, Pakistan and India, 1960s.

portrait.alt: Norman Borlaug at 90, white-haired, in a dark suit and dotted tie on a city street
portrait.credit: Norman Borlaug, 2004. Ben Zinner, USAID. Public domain.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Wheat that snapped
slides.text: Around 1960, West Pakistan fell short of wheat every year, and tall wheat snapped when fed more fertilizer. **Norman Borlaug's team set out to breed shorter wheat.**
slides.alt: A wheat field with a wide patch of tall stalks knocked flat to the ground
slides.credit: Wheat flattened by rain and wind, 2013. Azizkhan327. CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Short wheat, big harvests
slides.text: The dwarf wheat took two or three times the fertilizer and lifted top yields over 70 percent. **In 1968 India harvested a record 17 million tons.**
slides.alt: A broad field of ripe golden wheat beside a stretch of water under a cloudy sky in Punjab
slides.credit: Ripe wheat in Punjab, 2019. Harvinder Chandigarh. CC BY-SA 4.0.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Wells that keep getting deeper
slides.statLabel: of groundwater lost in northwest India, 2002 to 2008, one study found
slides.text: The seeds paid off with water, and Punjab filled with thirsty rice and wheat. **Farmers now drill 200 to 300 feet for water.**
slides.alt: A pump engine and pipe at a brick tube well beside a green wheat field
slides.credit: Tube well in Mansa district, Punjab, India, 2012. Tari Buttar. CC0.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: His worry was people, not water
slides.text: Punjab's water table was falling 18 cm a year by the mid-1980s. **Borlaug's own 1970 warning was about population, not water.**

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Still pumping more than it rains
slides.text: In 2010 Punjab pumped 45 percent more groundwater each year than rain put back. **The water bill is still arriving.**

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Developing-world cereal harvests tripled in 50 years on 30 percent more land (PNAS, 2012)
India's record wheat crop of 17 million tons in 1968
costs: 109 cubic kilometers of groundwater lost in northwest India, 2002 to 2008 (Nature, 2009)
Punjab pumping 45 percent more groundwater than rain puts back (Columbia Water Center, 2010)
Water use, soil damage and chemical runoff (PNAS, 2012)
slides.text: It gave cereal harvests that tripled across the developing world in 50 years. **It cost wells that keep getting deeper.**

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Cheap now, paid later
slides.text: The harvest pays every season, and flat-fee power made pumping more cost nothing extra. **The aquifer bill comes due over decades.**

slides.label: Lesson
slides.title: Price the resource your tool depends on
slides.text: A review found the damage came less from the seeds than from policies that made water cheap to overuse. **Price the resource your tool depends on.**
